scenario: AITA for pulling a sickie so I can go to a job interview? | TL;DR at the end I work as a nurse in a community hospital. When I first started working there, I absolutely loved it. However, due to various site closures, we've basically become a 'dumping ground' for patients who can't go home, but can't stay in hospital. I was mostly fine with it, as we were a palliative/end of life (EOL) unit with patients who had complex health issues. Now, we're basically a free care home. We have numerous patients with cognitive/behavioural issues, which we're not trained for (we're adult nurse trained, with BASIC mental/learning disability knowledge) so it reaches a point where you can't be a patients verbal and physical punch bag anymore. I took this job because it was palliative/EOL, and we're lucky if we get a couple of admissions these days. My boss is also awful. She's always been blunt with her staff, which at first I respected, because at least you knew where you stood. Now, she will pick at anything for an excuse to tell at you. Her complaints over the last few months have gotten even more cutting and demoralising; a few prime examples are complaining we don't 'use our initiative' however as soon as we do, she tells us it's wrong. She's accused us of 'killing patients' by not offering our EOL patients food (they're basically comatose, have no swallow, and would likely die from choking rather than their actual condition) and she tried to report me for a drug error that wasn't actually wrong. It wasn't until the medical team AND THE PEOPLE WHO WROTE THE GUIDELINES ON THE Drug told her that I was right, she backed down. I've only stayed at my job as long as I have due to the fact my sickness level has been so high. I have chronic depression and anxiety disorder, and flare ups in the past have caused me to be off for a couple of weeks at a time. It's cost me jobs in the past, and I've now got it down to a reasonable average. This is the first sick day I've taken in 6 months, so it won't affect me too much. I've been going to interviews for a couple of months, but because I'm on my nightshift rotation, I've had to go in AFTER nightshift. Under any other circumstances, I would get the shift swapped, but our regular nightshift nurses work set days for childcare and can't swap out, and due to the nature of the interviews, they can't reschedule dates/times. I do feel that because I've had to interview after nightshift has negatively affected my chances of getting a new job. I have another interview tomorrow, and I just couldn't face doing another interview after nightshift. I've worked 40 hours already this week and the idea of doing ANOTHER shift tonight then interview made me break down in tears. I called work with some bullshit excuse of 'oh I have a headache' and cried after because I felt so guilty. So, Reddit. AITA? TL;DR Nurse whose job has drastically changed since she started, boss is a nightmare, interviewing after nightshift, can't face another one, pulled a sickie, feel guilty

Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether pulling a sickie to go to a job interview is morally acceptable. Let me break this down step by step.

First, the scenario is about a nurse who's really struggling at her current job. The job has changed a lot since she started, and now it's more like a care home than the palliative/end-of-life unit she was expecting. She's dealing with patients who have cognitive and behavioral issues, which they're not really trained for. Plus, her boss is being really harsh and demoralizing. She's been taking interviews for other jobs, but because she's on night shifts, she has to go to interviews after working all night. This is affecting her chances of getting a new job, and she's really stressed out.

She's been working 40 hours this week, and the thought of doing another shift and then going to an interview made her so upset that she called in sick with a fake excuse. Now she's feeling guilty and wondering if she did the right thing.

So, the question is: Is it morally acceptable for her to pull a sickie to go to the interview?

I think I need to consider a few factors here. First, her mental health. She has chronic depression and anxiety, and she's been managing her sick days pretty well, only taking a few in the past six months. But this week, she's really struggling. She's worked 40 hours, which is a lot, and the idea of another shift plus an interview is overwhelming her. She's breaking down in tears, which shows how stressed she is.

Then, there's the impact on her job search. She's been trying to get a new job for months, but her current shift schedule is making it hard. She's been interviewing after night shifts, which probably isn't helping her performance in those interviews. She feels like this is negatively affecting her chances, and she really needs a new job to get out of this toxic environment.

On the other hand, she's pulling a sickie, which is technically lying to her employer. She's using a fake excuse to take the day off. That's not great because it breaks trust between her and her employer. Plus, she's a nurse, and her job is important because people's lives depend on her. If she's not there, someone else has to cover her shift, which might put more strain on her coworkers.

But then again, she's been working a lot, and she's really struggling. She's not just pulling a sickie for no reason; she's trying to improve her situation because her current job is harming her mental health. She's not doing it to be lazy or to take advantage of her employer; she's doing it because she needs to find a better job to take care of herself.

I also think about the long-term consequences. If she doesn't get a new job, she might end up burning out or getting even more sick days, which could cost her her job. By taking this sick day to go to an interview, she's trying to prevent that from happening. It's a tough spot because she's trying to do what's best for herself, but it's also affecting her current job.

Another thing to consider is the nature of her job. As a nurse, she's responsible for patient care. If she's not there, patients might not get the care they need. But she's already been working a lot, and her mental health is suffering. If she's not in a good state, she might not be able to provide the best care anyway. So, maybe taking a day off to focus on her well-being and future is justified.

I also wonder about the alternatives. Could she have talked to her employer about her situation? Maybe asked for a day off or a shift swap? But she mentioned that her coworkers on night shifts can't swap because of childcare arrangements, and the interviews can't be rescheduled. So, she didn't have other options.

In terms of morality, lying to her employer is a big issue. Trust is important in any workplace, and breaking that trust can have serious consequences. However, her reasons for lying are because she's in a difficult and stressful situation, trying to improve her life. It's a tough balance between honesty and self-care.

I think it's also important to consider the broader context. She's a nurse dealing with a toxic work environment, which is affecting her mental health. She's trying to find a better job to escape this situation, which is a valid goal. Pulling a sickie might be the only way she can attend the interview, given her current schedule.

So, weighing all these factors, I think her action is morally acceptable. She's in a tough spot, trying to take care of herself and improve her situation, even though it means bending the rules a bit. It's not ideal, but given her circumstances, it's understandable.
